confounds: Diagnosed users had more retained posts on average than controls (622.7 versus 526.5 per user); raw post counts are therefore unreliable. The analysis emphasized user prevalence and equal-weight per-user post shares.
Persistence was estimated from four source-order timeline bins, not actual calendar intervals; no temporal spacing was available.
Lexical self-context heuristics cannot perfectly resolve quotation, lyrics, jokes, sarcasm, advocacy, news, or discussion of another person.
Labels are outcomes to explain, not clinical ground truth; semantic associations should not be interpreted as diagnostic or causal.

Politics, news, sports, work, and study differences may reflect collection period, demographics, activity level, or public-versus-personal account mix.

negative_results: Generic relationship/family vocabulary was nearly universal and weakly discriminative; distress-anchored relationship and isolation language was more useful.
Humor was not absent among diagnosed users: it appeared for 98.1% diagnosed versus 96.0% controls, while normalized humor-post share was higher in controls (11.86% versus 9.34%).
Generic social-activity language did not favor diagnosed users: prevalence was 94.8% versus 95.8%, with slightly higher normalized share and persistence in controls.
Explicit diagnosis wording alone had substantial overlap: 46.9% diagnosed versus 39.6% controls; self-context and repetition were more informative.
Future-oriented language was not reduced in diagnosed users; planning and hopeful language were both common, alongside somewhat higher hopelessness markers.
Positive-affect vocabulary was near-universal and not specific; isolated physical-symptom words were also common in both groups.
